title: Decision Fatigue
description: The more decisions you make, the worse your subsequent decisions become. Willpower is a limited resource; after a day of choices, you default to whatever is easiest.
shortDescription: The more decisions you make, the worse your subsequent decisions become. Willpower is a limited resource; after a day of choices, you default to whatever is easiest.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: The more decisions you make, the worse your subsequent decisions become. Willpower is a limited resource; after a day of choices, you default to whatever is easiest.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: Judges grant parole more often in the morning than in the afternoon; decision fatigue makes them default to the safe, status‑quo choice (deny) as the day wears on (Danziger et al., 2011).
After a long day of shopping, you buy an expensive, unnecessary item because you’re too tired to resist.
At the end of a long workday, you skip the gym and order takeaway because choosing a healthy meal feels like too much effort.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Simplifying choices by going with the default or doing nothing.
Impulse purchases late in the day.
Snapping at others because emotional regulation is drained along with decision energy.
Making rushed, low‑quality decisions to “just get it done.”

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “I can’t deal with this right now.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You’re putting off important decisions because you’re mentally exhausted.
Your choices later in the day are consistently worse or more indulgent.
You avoid making any decision after a certain point.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Decision‑making consumes glucose in the prefrontal cortex. As resources deplete, the brain shifts to lower‑effort strategies. (The exact metabolic mechanism is debated, but the behavioral effect is robust.)

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Make important decisions early in the day.
Structure your day to minimize trivial decisions (e.g., meal prep, clothing choice simplified).
If you must decide later, first replenish with a break, a snack, or a walk to reset.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Scheduling critical meetings at 4 p.m. after a full day of decisions.
Assuming you can “power through” and maintain decision quality; you can’t.
Judging yourself harshly for “lazy” choices when you’re simply depleted.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A CEO stacks critical strategic decisions in the last hour of the day because “that’s when I have time.” The team notices that approvals in the morning are more thoughtful; in the late afternoon, the CEO rubber‑stamps or rejects quickly without analysis. The company’s direction is shaped by when the meeting happened more than by the content.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: Your decision‑making is a battery, not a power cord. It drains with every choice. Recharge before you short‑circuit.
